label: Polars Of Convex Sets
notes: Open by presenting polarity as a change in what is being stored. The primal set stores points, while the polar stores linear tests whose value never exceeds one on those points. Keep the phrase reciprocal halfspace constraints in view; every later theorem is a disciplined way of intersecting, reversing, or recovering from those tests.

label: Inequality Definition
notes: Do the definition slowly. A candidate y is not in the polar because it looks near the origin; it is in the polar only if the support value of C in direction y is at most one. For finite examples, students can test every vertex. For general closed convex bodies, the support function packages the same universal inequality.

label: Unit Ball Examples
notes: Use the gallery to inoculate against the idea that polars are just scaled copies. The Euclidean ball is self-polar, but the square becomes the diamond and an ellipse swaps long and short axes. Each picture is a support-value statement: the farthest primal point in the candidate dual direction must stop at level one.

label: Polygon Polar
notes: Read the polygon picture from left to right. Each primal vertex x_i contributes the halfspace of all y with pairing at most one. The polar polygon is the intersection of those reciprocal halfspaces. Point out that a facet of one side often corresponds to a vertex or active inequality on the other side.

label: Order Reversal
notes: Order reversal is a logic statement, not a visual trick. If A is contained in B, then every y that passes all tests on B automatically passes all tests on A. Larger primal sets impose more inequalities, so their polar sets are smaller. Use the disk-inside-square row to make the reversal concrete.

label: Bipolar Theorem Picture
notes: State the bipolar theorem as a reconstruction promise with hypotheses attached. From C to C polar we keep all valid level-one tests. Applying the same operation again intersects all halfspaces supported by those tests. If C is closed, convex, and contains the origin, no information is lost; otherwise the operation repairs the set.

label: Cones And Dual Cones
notes: For cones, let scaling do the algebra. The level-one bound can hold for all positive multiples only when the pairing has the correct sign. With the sign convention on the slide, the set polar of a cone is the negative of the usual nonnegative dual cone. That distinction prevents later sign errors.

label: Lineality And Full Dimension
notes: This is the rank and lineality bookkeeping slide. A line inside a primal cone forces the polar cone to live in the orthogonal subspace, because both directions along the line must satisfy the sign test. For closed cones, pointedness and full dimension trade places under duality. Pause here because many separation arguments secretly rely on exactly this bookkeeping.

label: Gauge Support Connection
notes: Connect polarity to quantities students have already seen. The support function h_C asks how far C reaches in a direction. The polar is the sublevel set where that reach is at most one. Conversely, when C is closed, convex, and absorbs the direction under study, the gauge of C is the support function of C polar.

label: Halfspace Reconstruction
notes: Halfspace reconstruction is the operational version of the bipolar theorem. Imagine storing a set not by drawing it but by listing every valid polar normal. To query whether x belongs to the recovered body, test all those normals. If x sits outside a closed convex C containing the origin, separation supplies a polar normal that rejects it.

label: Numerical Polar Sampling
notes: Treat the sampling table as a tiny executable polar test. The accepted candidates have maximum dot product below one across the listed vertices; the rejected candidates have a named active vertex that breaks the threshold. Stress that sampling alone is not a theorem for arbitrary sets, but finite polytopes let vertex checks certify the inequality.

label: Failure Without Closure Origin
notes: Use the two failures to show what the bipolar operation remembers. An open disk has the same polar as its closure, because support uses a supremum rather than an attained maximum. A set away from the origin reconstructs with the origin adjoined and convexified. The theorem is not failing; the hypotheses describe exactly what information polarity preserves.

label: Rule Ledger
notes: Read the ledger as a checklist for future sections. The left column names the operation, the middle column gives the polar effect, and the right column names the likely trap. The purpose is practical: when a proof starts with a polar, students should know which inclusion, closure, sign, or gauge convention is being used.

label: Recap
notes: Close by returning to the central mental model. A polar is a database of reciprocal halfspace constraints. Inclusion reverses because databases get stricter. Bipolar recovery works because all valid tests cut out the original closed convex body containing the origin. The examples show how balls, polytopes, cones, and gauges all speak this same language.
